topic.title: The generous return window
topic.claim: The 30-day no-questions return policy isn't kindness; it's a bet that you won't send it back, and you almost never do.
topic.moment: You keep the slightly-wrong kurta because returning it means printing a label and finding a pickup slot.

turn.believed: A long return window means the brand trusts its product and respects you.
turn.actually: They've counted that most people never return anything, so the promise costs them little and closes the sale for them.

topic.because: A visible safety net removes the last doubt at checkout, and human laziness guarantees most returns never happen. The brand keeps your money and your trust.
topic.payoff: The easier they make returns on paper, the more they're counting on you not bothering.
topic.behaviour: Brands advertise easy returns prominently while quietly relying on low actual return rates to boost conversion.
topic.mechanism: The promise closes the sale; inertia means it rarely gets used.
topic.group: online shoppers who buy clothes and gadgets on apps
topic.send_to: the friend with three unworn things still in their boxes, because the return date passed
topic.why_now: Festive sale returns are piling up and most people are letting the window close.

score.why: Everyone has the unreturned kurta; the turn, the easy return window is a bet you won't bother, is a sharp dark pattern with a built-in test.

ledger.text: Most shoppers who intend to return an ill-fitting or wrong item within a long return window never actually complete the return, due to the friction and procrastination involved, so brands keep the sale revenue while appearing generous
ledger.sentence: They advertise returns loud and rely on almost nobody using them. The promise closes the sale; your laziness keeps their money and your goodwill.

mechanism.broken_premise: The causal premise is only partly right. The post pins non-returns on 'friction and procrastination' ('your laziness keeps their money'). The strongest primary evidence (Janakiraman, Syrdal & Freling's 2016 Journal of Retailing meta-analysis of 21 studies) finds that *time* leniency — a longer window — reduces returns mainly through the endowment effect: the longer you hold an item, the more attached you get and the more you talk yourself into keeping it. It also separates the mechanisms the post merges: it is *monetary* and *low-effort* leniency that lift purchases, while the *long window* is what suppresses returns — so the window is doing the retention work more than the conversion work the post credits it with.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: A generous policy does boost sales and most items never come back (US ecommerce return rates run ~17–25%, so the large majority are kept), which is exactly the asymmetry the post describes. But the dominant reason long windows cut returns is psychological ownership, not just inertia: time to bond with the product plus genuine friction (labels, pickups) both push the keep-rate up, and retailers knowingly tune these levers — long windows to reduce returns, easy refunds to win the sale. Net effect matches the take: the promise closes the sale and few redeem it.

sources.quote: leniency in time reduced return rates ... attributed to the endowment effect, whereby consumers develop stronger attachment to products they possess longer ... lenient return policies led to increased purchases
lengthening the return window reduces returns, via the endowment effect, while reducing the effort required to return increases purchases
the average U.S. ecommerce return rate was around 20.4% in 2024 ... apparel return rates run roughly 25%

_ledger.text:
[cover] A 30-day return window is a bet you'll never [bother]
That easy-returns promise feels like respect. Watch what you actually do with it.
 

[slide 1] A 30-day return window is a bet you'll never bother.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] The kurta arrives and it's a little off. Tight at the shoulder, the colour a shade louder than the app promised.
No stress. Thirty days, no questions. You'll send it back this weekend.

[slide 3] And buying from them felt good in the first place. A brand this relaxed about returns clearly trusts its own stuff.
That's the read they wanted you to have.

[slide 4] The box sits by the door. Returning it means printing a label, booking a pickup slot, keeping an afternoon free for a delivery guy who comes whenever.
Day 31. The return button is gone. The brand had this exact outcome priced in the day they wrote "easy returns."

[slide 5] The long window was never about trust. It was the last doubt removed at checkout, the line that made your thumb stop hovering and tap buy.
They advertise returns loud and rely on almost nobody using them. The promise closes the sale; your laziness keeps their money and your goodwill.

[slide 6] Count the things in your cupboard with the tags still on. Each one is a bet the brand placed on you, and won.

[end card] Open this again the next time a return window is about to close on you.
Send it to the friend with three unworn things still in their boxes, return date long gone.

[caption] What's the one thing sitting in its box right now, tags on, because you never got around to printing the label?

[alt text] A six-slide carousel arguing that a generous 30-day return policy is a sales tactic, not kindness. It follows a reader who buys a slightly-wrong kurta online, trusts the relaxed return promise, keeps meaning to send it back, and lets the window close, showing that brands advertise easy returns while relying on customer inertia to keep both the money and the goodwill.
